newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Key points of South Korea's new labour law.
newsitem.headline: Key points of South Korea's new labour law.

text.p: South Korea's parliament on Monday passed a revised labour bill to replace a law that sparked almost one month of strikes after its forced passage last December.
Following are the key components of the new legislation (with the December law in brackets).

Postpones until 1999 implementation of a clause making it easier for companies to lay off workers. When the provision takes effect, companies will be allowed to shed staff during a "management emergency". There is no definition of what constitutes an emergency. (Management can lay off workers in cases of corporate restructuring, introduction of new technology, change in the business line, to boost productivity, as a result of a business downturn or mergers and acquisitions.)
Multiple unions permitted at a national level immediately and at a company level by 2002. (Multiple unions on a national level from 2000 and company level from 2002.)
Employers may replace strikers from within the company, but not from outside. They may not subcontract work during strikes. (Strikers may be replaced with other workers from similar businesses.)
Employers have no obligation to pay strikers. Unions face fines if they strike to demand such pay. (Employers banned from paying strikers. Unions cannot strike to demand such pay.)
Employers are banned from paying full-time union officials from 2002. (No change.)
Employers may introduce flexible work hours according to a formula that caps total working hours per day, week and month. (Flexible hours, but no cap on the working day.)
Sacked workers retain union membership until a second appeal against their dismissal to the Central Labour Relations Commission. (Union membership until the first appeal.)

The government may force arbitration on strikers in key public sectors, including railways, subways, city buses, freight, utilities, hospitals, telecommunications and banks. From 2001 city buses and banks, excluding the central Bank of Korea, will no longer be categorised as a key public sector. The three largest parties agreed to discuss allowing teachers and civil servants to join unions. (The December bill excludes the clause making exceptions for bus services and banks by 2001.)
